title: Learning Interaction Dynamics via Motion-Region Guidance for Robotic Video World Models
summary: Action-conditioned video world models imagine future observations under candidate robot actions, providing a promising visual tool for robot policy evaluation and interaction simulation. However, existing video world models often optimize global reconstruction errors instead of emphasizing interaction-relevant regions. As a result, they may preserve overall scene appearance but overlook local interaction details, leading to physically implausible outcomes such as hallucinated contact effects and inconsistent robot-object interactions. We introduce MoReWorld, a unified motion-region-guided framework that uses a shared motion region, the part of the environment that moves in response to the robot's actions, to focus dynamics learning and video generation on interaction-relevant regions. The same motion region guides local motion prediction, region-aware supervision, and motion-gated future-feature conditioning. At inference time, the motion region is predicted as a motion probability map from visual history and robot actions, without requiring future observations or ground-truth motion labels. On WorldSimProbe, MoReWorld achieves the highest overall simulator-faithfulness score, with the strongest performance on local consistency, global consistency, and interaction dynamics. These results indicate that motion-region guidance helps the model preserve scene-level consistency while more faithfully predicting action-conditioned interaction dynamics.

title: EgoLAM: Learning Latent Actions from Hand and Head Motion
summary: Latent action models let a robot policy learn from video by turning the change between two frames into a training target. In egocentric video, a cup can move across the image because a hand pushes it or because the wearer turns. Both changes help predict the next frame, but only the first describes manipulation. During training, EgoLAM supervises the action code with measured wrist motion and supplies camera motion separately to the forward model. Even when the wearer turns while pushing a cup, the training target still describes how the hand pushed it. The action encoder pools object slots around each hand, and wrist translation and rotation can be decoded from the code in a common reference frame. Extracting a code then requires only two RGB frames. Alongside LARYBench classification and regression, we measure how much wrist motion a frozen code retains and how strongly it responds to a synthetic view or lighting change. EgoLAM has the highest hand-motion decoding score among eight evaluated models. Across three LIBERO suites, policies pretrained on its codes and fine-tuned on expert demonstrations achieve 79.38% mean success, 28.73 points above expert behavior cloning and 9.76 points above the strongest other latent action model in each suite on average.

title: Show Me the Answer: Visual Grounding on Dashboards
summary: Natural language interaction has become an increasingly important paradigm for accessing complex visual information systems. In visual data analytics environments, such as dashboards, a key capability is to ground user queries to specific visual elements, enabling systems to identify the visual evidence relevant to the query. However, existing visual grounding research has primarily focused on natural images, while grounding in dashboards remains underexplored due to their complex multi-chart layouts and fine-grained visual elements. In this paper, we study the task of Visual Grounding on Dashboards (VGD): Given a dashboard screenshot and a natural language query, the goal is to localize the visual element corresponding to the query using a bounding box. We propose VGD-Net, a two-stage grounding framework that reflects how users typically locate information in dashboards, by first performing query-aware chart retrieval and then fine-grained in-chart grounding. To systematically evaluate VGD-Net's performance on this task, we construct VGD-Bench, a benchmark specifically designed for VGD, covering three complementary settings: chart retrieval, in-chart grounding, and overall VGD. Experimental results show that our two-stage VGD-Net outperforms strong multimodal baselines on the VGD task, achieving a mean IoU of 57.06 and a success rate of 66.82, while also delivering superior performance over existing methods in both stages of chart retrieval and in-chart grounding. These results highlight the value of stage decomposition for reliable and interpretable VGD, and its potential to support query-driven visual analysis.

title: Can Reasoning and Image Description Enhance Yes/No Visual Mathematical Understanding?
summary: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on general visual tasks, yet their ability to understand mathematical images remains limited. This paper investigates whether explicit reasoning and textual image descriptions can enhance VLMs' performance on binary yes/no visual mathematical questions. To achieve this, we curated a paired evaluation set to benchmark prominent open-source VLMs under varying prompt and input conditions. In particular, we leverage Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting and use textual descriptions, either replacing or augmenting visual inputs, to isolate and evaluate mathematical comprehension. Our results show that explicit reasoning improves performance, especially in paired consistency accuracy, while textual image descriptions do not consistently help and may degrade performance. These findings suggest that reasoning is important for stable visual mathematical judgement, whereas description-based intermediates require more careful design.

title: HR-Merge: Model Merging with Headroom-Weighted Residual Refinement
comment: 21 pages, 7 figures, 16 tables. A short version was accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Neural Network Artifacts as a New Data Modality
summary: Model merging combines experts fine-tuned from a shared backbone, such as LoRA adapters of a large language model, into one multi-task model without further training. Existing methods apply one rule to every task, yet the accuracy they lose is uneven across tasks. We show that the lost accuracy remains recoverable from each task's residual, its task vector minus the merged update, and that a task's validation headroom, the share of its expert validation accuracy the merge loses, indicates where recovery pays off. Residuals from different tasks interfere, so they must be merged rather than summed. We propose HR-Merge, a training-free wrapper around any merging method. It weights each residual by its task's headroom, re-merges the weighted residuals with the base operator, and adds the result back at a strength selected on validation, falling back to the base merge when no strength helps. On six NLI adapters of LLaMA-3 8B, HR-Merge lifts TIES from 93.29 to 94.29 normalized accuracy, above all tested bases, mainly by recovering its weakest task. In vision, on three CLIP backbones, up to 20 tasks, and LoRA merging, it generally improves or preserves base accuracy and yields the best model in every setting.

title: A Framework for AI-Ready Data in Earth and Environmental Science
comment: 12 pages excluding appendixes. Submitted to Earth System Science Data (ESSD), Oct 2026
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI), specifically machine learning (ML), is increasingly integral to Earth and environmental research, yet the suitability of current research data infrastructures for supporting AI workflows remains poorly defined. While the FAIR principles provide a foundation for scientific data management, they do not explicitly address several requirements arising when datasets are used for training, evaluating, and deploying AI models. This article presents a practically motivated framework for assessing and improving AI-readiness of research data within distributed Earth and environmental data infrastructures. The framework was developed through a structured, community-driven process, beginning with a review of existing literature and readiness frameworks combined with feedback from a limited survey of scientists applying ML methods. Its main aspects were shaped by a multidisciplinary expert group representing data providers, infrastructure developers, data managers, and AI practitioners. It identifies 25 criteria covering data preparation, data quality, documentation, access, and supervised learning targets. The criteria emphasize aspects particularly relevant to AI applications, including provenance, treatment of missing data, bias documentation, uncertainty characterization, machine-actionable metadata, efficient access formats, and the quality and reproducibility of target generation. Application to a broad range of representative environmental use cases highlights how the relevance of individual criteria varies by application. We argue that AI-readiness should be understood primarily as a property of transparency and fitness for purpose rather than as a fixed level of data quality. The framework lays a foundation for communication and community-driven action to advance AI-ready data and support next-generation AI-enabled scientific workflows.

title: TrojanMaxxing: One-shotting VLM Backdoors with Weight-Space Programming
summary: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can reason directly about the weights of other neural networks. Given only a natural-language objective, an LLM can inspect a model's weights, understand what they compute, and edit them directly without gradient-based optimization. This capability, termed weight-space programming (WSP), has been used to improve model performance on math reasoning, medical QA and other benchmarks. We propose TrojanMaxxing, a novel strategy to backdoor vision-language models (VLMs), by reframing it as a WSP task. We use Claude Opus 5.5 and Mythos 5.2 agents to backdoor VLMs without any optimization or training methods. The agents inspect the model weights, apply targeted edits, and co-design an imperceptible visual trigger that activates the backdoor. We then study the agents' strategies and present a thorough evaluation of the trojaned models on various benchmark datasets. TrojanMaxxing achieves attack success rates of 93%-100% on content moderation and 78%-100% on OCR while maintaining clean accuracy. Perhaps most consequentially, we show that injecting backdoors in a training-free manner is possible by simply, "asking an agent to do it".

title: Do Language Models Know Which Words Steer Their Reasoning?
summary: While chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting elicits intermediate reasoning steps from language models, it is unclear which words in the context actually steer the CoT. We identify Phantom Context Influence (PCI): language models are disproportionately steered by semantically irrelevant context words, even as the same models deny those words' relevance when asked. To localize PCI, we introduce Leave-One-Out Word JSD analysis, which removes one context word at a time from the otherwise intact context to isolate its marginal effect on the next-token distribution; words whose removal flips the prediction (pivot words) are passed to the same LLM to self-judge whether it recognizes this predictive dependence. Across four models and three benchmarks, language models largely do not know which words steer their reasoning, a mismatch we call the Generation-Judgment Contradiction. Inspired by this phenomenon, we propose Online KV Suppression: it scores every prompt word's influence over the whole chain of thought in a single pass, then zeroes the KV-cache entries of the highest-influence word the model itself judges inert and redecodes. This single-word intervention improves CoT accuracy across four models and five reasoning benchmarks, by up to 8.9 percentage points on math reasoning benchmark.

title: Neurodegenerative Differential Diagnosis with Knowledge-enhanced Structural Reasoning
summary: Accurate differential diagnosis of neurodegenerative disorders remains challenging due to overlapping clinical manifestations and heterogeneous, often incomplete multimodal observations. Existing multimodal models can integrate imaging and clinical measurements but often overlook disease-specific evidence patterns and pairwise relations among competing diagnoses. We therefore propose Knowledge-enhanced Structural Reasoning (KnowSR), which aligns multimodal patient representations with a literature-grounded knowledge bank of disease prototypes, signed evidence directions, and pairwise diagnostic relations. Specifically, in KnowSR, patient-specific knowledge alignment and target-aware pooling inject structured disease evidence, while anchored relational reasoning reconciles pairwise diagnostic margins over a sparse differential graph, thereby collectively enhancing differential diagnostic capability. Across extensive experiments, KnowSR consistently outperforms 19 baselines on patient-level six-class diagnosis under patient-disjoint five-fold evaluation. This shows that grounding patient evidence in structured medical knowledge enables more effective differential diagnosis than naive multimodal fusion alone.

title: Reasoning in Fewer Tokens: Concept-Normalized Multilingual Scratchpads and Reversible Model-Adaptive Reasoning Codes
summary: Chain-of-thought prompting significantly improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) but incurs high inference costs due to lengthy autoregressive decoding. While previous efficiency approaches reduce costs by discarding tokens or utilizing continuous latent representations, these lossy methods fundamentally sacrifice interpretability and auditability. In this work, we introduce a novel compression framework for intermediate reasoning. We apply Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) to reasoning corpora to learn a compressed vocabulary of Private Use Area (PUA) tokens, each representing frequent semantic spans. After expanding the LLM's vocabulary, we fine-tune the model via strictly 1:1, our method is lossless. We evaluate our approach on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-14B, and Qwen2.5-32B across four diverse benchmarks. Our method reduces total generated tokens by 14.7% on average with reasoning trace lengths dropping by up to 27.1%, while incurring a negligible average accuracy cost of 1.6 percentage points. Crucially, this approach is orthogonal to existing lossy methods, allowing practitioners to stack lossless and irreversible compression techniques. We demonstrate that a compressed intermediate language provides a highly efficient computational resource that accelerates inference while fully preserving the transparency of LLM reasoning.

title: Mechanism Parity for Simulation-Based Validation of Autonomous-Driving Perception
comment: 15 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Extended version of the authors' papers at IEEE IV 2026 and IEEE ITSC 2026. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Simulation is central to intelligent-vehicle validation, but visual realism or output agreement between a real scene and its synthetic counterpart does not prove that a perception system used the same evidence in both domains. This paper addresses that mechanism-parity gap for paired real-synthetic autonomous-driving perception. It unifies Decisive-Feature Fidelity, which compares decisive evidence maps in a frozen system under test (SUT), with Concept-Decisive Feature Fidelity, which projects decisive evidence into semantic scene concepts for diagnosis. The framework is a validation diagnostic rather than a standalone safety certificate: it asks whether output-consistent simulation also preserves the mechanism by which the perception model reaches that output. The empirical evidence comprises ten retrained diffusion ControlNet generators evaluated on a deterministic exact-geometry KITTI-Virtual KITTI 2 subset. Generated counterparts use a 1248-by-376-pixel padded inference canvas and are cropped back to the exact KITTI dimensions before evaluation. The final benchmark reports target-image, output-consistency, and mechanism metrics recomputed from a single audited output set, then adds metric-disagreement cases, bootstrap uncertainty, threshold sensitivity, and concept/cache integrity audits. Across the benchmark, output and appearance fidelity are at most weakly and inconsistently rank-correlated with decisive-mechanism distance for all three frozen SUTs, and a constructed positive control shows the estimator detects a known planted mechanism that output agreement misses, supporting decisive-evidence diagnostics for intelligent-vehicle simulation validation. All numerical claims are restricted to the declared exact-geometry benchmark, ten generators, and three frozen SUTs.

title: Unimodal Shortcuts and Joint Scene-Intent Dependence in Vision-Language Safety Representations
comment: 39 pages, 8 figures, 18 tables (14 pages main paper, 25 pages supplementary material)
summary: The safety of a request to a vision-language model often depends on the image: asking how to serve a dish is harmless for fresh food and harmful for spoiled food. High accuracy on situational safety benchmarks does not tell us whether a model's safety representation encodes both the scene and the user's intent, because a benchmark can often be solved from one modality alone. Studying frozen vision-language safety representations, we audit five public situational benchmarks and find that each admits a unimodal shortcut: images alone predict the labels, and on same-image prompt pairs a probe that never sees the photograph reaches 0.9645 AUROC. We therefore build a controlled evaluation that crosses safe and hazardous scenes with observation and action requests, so that no single-modality rule can exceed 0.500 group-ranking accuracy. On this control, linear probes on intermediate states of Qwen3-VL-8B and SmolVLM2-2.2B reach 0.958 and 0.930, showing that the scene-intent conjunction is linearly decodable; concatenating separately encoded image and text states already recovers most of this signal, so decodability is not evidence of a fusion mechanism. The same probes screen cheaply but generalize poorly to unseen images and other benchmarks. Reliable multimodal safety evaluation therefore needs controls that rule out unimodal shortcuts before accuracy is read as evidence of joint understanding.

title: ROSWORLD: When Digital Task Competence Meets Physical Execution
summary: Computer-use agents now solve most desktop tasks through direct software input, but a robot using the same computer must turn GUI knowledge into physical contact with a keyboard and mouse. We introduce ROSWorld, a benchmark that couples a physically simulated robot workstation to a live OSWorld desktop, so that a robot and a desktop agent pursue the same goals under the same official evaluators. The evaluated model receives observations only from the workstation camera views and operates the peripherals through either a single-arm rigid probe or dual-arm dexterous hands. Across five frontier models and 40 tasks in ten applications, models that complete 31-39 tasks on the desktop complete at most 23 with the probe and 28 with the hands. Paired trajectory analysis shows that models adapt their interaction strategies toward keyboard input, yet physical execution frequently fails through missed presses, incorrect targets, and unintended contacts. ROSWorld makes the gap between knowing what to do on a computer and physically doing it measurable.

title: From Tokens to Pixels: Training-Free Guided Upsampling of Frozen CARL Features for Hyperspectral Imaging
comment: 17 pages, 16 figures, 5 tables. Code and result tables: https://gitlab.fb10.fh-dortmund.de/fb10-opensource/CARL-tokens-to-pixels
summary: Camera-agnostic foundation models such as CARL map spectral images from arbitrary sensors into a shared feature space, but deliver their features only on a token grid at one eighth of the input resolution. The usual bilinear interpolation blurs material boundaries over about one token and rounds off corners. We investigate how much spatial accuracy image-guided upsampling recovers for frozen CARL features without training the encoder or the upsampler. We compare joint bilateral upsampling (JBU), a guided filter and the pretrained AnyUp, each with the hyperspectral image or an RGB rendering as the guide. A hyperspectral ColorChecker dataset acquired specifically for this study, with model-independent reference geometry measured to sub-pixel precision, serves as the evaluation benchmark. JBU with the hyperspectral guide raises the Boundary IoU from 13 to 67 % and reduces the effective edge width of the features from 38 to 4 px, close to the resolution of the raw spectra. The effect occurs in all 24 patches of the ColorChecker and replicates on an additional recording. On placenta and oral cavity images, the feature edges also become markedly qualitatively sharper. For sharp, high-contrast boundaries, JBU is the most accurate and most economical method. On tissue with softer transitions, the pretrained AnyUp yields qualitatively sharper contours. An analysis of 78 simulated band configurations shows that the gain persists in every configuration as long as the head matches the configuration. Image-guided upsampling is thus a simple, training-free step for applications that use CARL frozen with linear heads.

title: PAVE: A Harness for Geometrically Consistent Road Network Modeling with Vision-Language Models
summary: Transportation models, whether they simulate traffic or support planning, are only as reliable as the road networks they run on, down to the lanes and turns at each intersection. Practitioners still take such a network from GIS files and supply its junction and movement data by hand, a task that recurs with each new base year and design alternative, or they generate it from open map data. OpenStreetMap's lane tags give the correct layout for only 13 of the 44 approaches we test; open map data are often incomplete or inaccurate. Satellite and street-level imagery, in contrast, cover all 44 and show their lanes as painted. Vision-language models (VLMs) can read such imagery, but asked directly they lose geometric consistency when the same lane must be matched across a satellite crop, street-level photos taken from different poses and an ID-labelled network. We therefore present PAVE (Perceive, Anchor, Verify, Edit), a harness in which code measures what can be measured, traffic engineering knowledge enters as general rules and checks, and the model makes only the open judgements, each anchored to network IDs so that checks catch answers that contradict a measurement, a second reading or a traffic rule. Scored against human labels at signalised intersections, PAVE raises the share of exactly correct lane layouts from 49-64% with a single request to 86-91% for two VLMs, with most of the gain coming from reading one approach at a time on traced lanes. The same division of work edits a real network to a planning brief: the model names the links and nodes of each part of a facility, and code builds the edit from a design template. Of 18 edits, 16 pass every network check, against none when the model writes its own code, and 2 contain a design or coding error, against 7. An analysis shows where VLMs lose geometric consistency and which check catches each failure.

title: Seeing Is Not Steering: Where Verifiable Reasoning Can Enter an End-to-End Driving Planner
summary: Driving models that reason may describe a hazard correctly while choosing their path for other reasons. We study where scene reasoning can enter an end-to-end planner so its influence can be checked. We freeze Drive-JEPA and use a fine-tuned vision-language model to state scene facts. Although fine-tuning improves fact accuracy, the two learned components we test show no detectable benefit from reading them. A rule-based fact check instead rejects or shortens paths that contradict the facts, linking each intervention to a stated fact. On the frozen planner alone, it gains 2.4 EPDMS points on navhard. Its 2.0-point margin over a control that changes the same frames without consulting facts remains statistically uncertain. A diagnostic using exact facts from maps and annotations yields a 3.6-point margin over its corresponding control, with a 95% confidence interval above zero. Separately, a path scorer and plan memory that read no stated facts raise navhard from 41.2 to 51.8. Bounding travel distance using the reasoner's facts adds 0.3 there and reduces navtest by 2.0. The fact check makes each intervention auditable, while the driving value of the reasoner's facts remains unresolved.

title: WaXup: Weight Averaging of Experts as Data Augmentation for Robust Introspection
summary: As the capabilities of large language models keep improving, traditional mechanistic interpretability methods struggle to keep pace. In contrast, trainable introspection methods emerge as a promising alternative; they repurpose the model itself as a self-diagnostic tool, trained to verbalize what it has learned during finetuning in natural language. While training on datasets of finetuned experts achieves encouraging results, it currently lacks robustness and generalization. Building on the data augmentation framework of MiXup, we introduce WaXup, a method that augments the introspection training set through linear interpolation in the weight space. This is motivated by the linear mode connectivity property: weight averaged experts interpolate the behaviors of the initial experts. We evaluate WaXup on three benchmarks: hidden-behavior models, a meta-dataset of real-world NLP tasks and AuditBench, a challenging alignment auditing suite of models adversarially trained to conceal their behaviors. WaXup improves the accuracy of generated descriptions as well as robustness to various distribution shifts. We hope to improve the reliability of trainable introspection methods towards better and safer models.

title: SOAR: Training-Free Rank-Consistent Rollout Compression for Latent World Model Planning
comment: 16 pages, including supplementary material. Anqi Li and Kai Liu contributed equally
summary: Latent world models plan by rolling out hundreds of candidate action sequences through a transformer predictor, so a single decision can take tens of seconds. Existing accelerations prune spatial tokens as in vision-language models, yet a sampling-based planner uses predicted costs only to rank candidates, so a rollout can be compressed freely as long as the ranking survives. We propose SOAR, a training-free method that adapts rollout compression to each planning decision. At every decision, SOAR probes a few candidates under several token budgets and keeps the smallest budget that preserves their ranking, so it compresses as far as the current decision allows, without task labels. A closed-loop study of more than 80,000 episodes fixes the rest of the rollout: the first step, which alone reads a real observation, stays exact, and the context frame is cached rather than recomputed. On seven navigation and manipulation tasks with frozen checkpoints, SOAR matches dense-level planning success at 2.3x speedup and retains 98% at 2.5x. Our code is available at https://github.com/starrywiki/SOAR.

title: Testing for Coordination Failures in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: Deep parallel cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (CMARL)} trains multiple agents that all act at every time step to optimize a common objective. Like single-agent RL, CMARL can produce unsafe behaviors that violate implicit safety requirements not captured by the reward, and these behaviors are hard to explain. However, testing CMARL policies for safety has received less attention than the safety testing of single-agent RL policies. In this paper, we propose DisQ, a test case selection method that identifies failure-revealing states in value-based CMARL by exploiting a signal specific to trained Q-learning agents. The signal is the Q-value gap, an explainable metric that flags a state when the agents' estimates of the achievable return diverge by more than a calibrated threshold. DisQ selects such states for execution and skips those without a gap. Our experiments in four CMARL benchmark environments show that, in most of the evaluated configurations, DisQ improves failure detection over single-agent RL testing methods applied to CMARL, namely random testing and search-based testing with genetic algorithms. Our main contributions are the Q-value gap, an indicator of potential miscoordination computable from a single state without executing the system, and DisQ, a test case selection method that adapts existing single-agent testing methods to CMARL.

title: Beyond Resolution: Inference-Time Parameterized Temporal Consistency in Generative Regional Climate Downscaling
summary: GCM-to-RCM downscaling emulation is dominated by generative diffusion models, but most existing work evaluates skill only per timestep, treating each field as an independent snapshot. This leaves open whether generated sequences are temporally coherent or merely independently plausible, a gap that matters increasingly for sub-daily resolutions since downstream impacts depend on accumulation and persistence, not just on isolated states. This study asks whether autoregressive conditioning can deliver coherent rollouts without error accumulation and ensemble-spread collapse, and whether a single model can expose the resulting coherence-diversity trade-off as a controllable inference choice rather than a fixed design commitment. We introduce a noise-conditioned teacher-forcing training scheme conditioning a diffusion U-Net downscaling model on a noised previous high-resolution state, so the trained model interpolates continuously between autoregressive (AR) and per-timestep independent (PTI) sampling via one noise parameter. We apply the scheme to an hourly, European-domain historical simulation downscaling AWI-CM1 (1$^\circ$) with ICON (0.11$^\circ$, regridded to 0.25$^\circ$) for precipitation and 2-meter temperature. The noise parameter traces a smooth interpolation between ICON's autocorrelation and PTI generation. AR rollouts of up to six months show no progressive degradation, with ensemble spread contracting only slightly within the first 24 hours. In contrast, the same architecture trained on noise-free previous states diverges. For precipitation PTI underestimates maxima by up to 2x in daily aggregations, while AR tracks ICON's maxima closely. For temperature, differences between modes are negligible. These results show that in diffusion downscaling temporal consistency can be achieved architecture-agnostically and offered as a controllable, not fixed, inference choice.

title: VMSA: Video Memory Skill Agent for Long Video Understanding
summary: Long-video question answering requires retrieving and integrating relevant evidence from videos spanning hours or even days. Recent agentic approaches organize video information into external memories and iteratively retrieve evidence to answer questions. However, effective retrieval and reasoning remain challenging, as agents must determine what information to search for, which memory sources to access, and how to connect evidence across distant temporal intervals. To address these challenges, we propose Video Memory Skill Agent (VMSA), a framework that jointly designs structured video memories and memory skills for long-video understanding. VMSA constructs three complementary memory components. Segment Caption Memory and Entity Event Memory serve as searchable evidence sources, while Entity-Aware Episode Memory provides broad yet detailed video context to guide evidence retrieval and reasoning. To further support effective memory utilization, VMSA induces memory skills from successful agent trajectories, incrementally refining or extending a compact skill library to guide iterative evidence retrieval, reasoning, and verification. Across seven long-video question-answering benchmarks, VMSA achieves the highest accuracy on all three week-long egocentric benchmarks, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 9.4% on Ego-R1 Bench, and the best or competitive performance on four additional benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of all three memory components and memory skills, with memory skills also improving temporal evidence localization.

title: Beyond Sample Hardness: Adaptive Data Selection through Learning Dynamics
summary: Data selection has emerged as an effective approach to reducing the model training costs. However, most existing methods often rely heavily on sample hardness, which may overlook differences in sample learning dynamics and lead to suboptimal sample selection. In this paper, we propose LeDAS, an end-to-end Learning Dynamics-Aware Selection framework for dynamic data selection, which jointly characterizes sample importance through hardness, learning progress, and deterioration, enabling adaptive sample prioritization throughout training with marginal additional computational overhead. Specifically, we track per-sample loss dynamics using exponential moving averages (EMA) to obtain three complementary signals that capture current learning difficulty, ongoing learning improvements, and potential degradation. To accommodate evolving training dynamics, we introduce Adaptive Metric Fusion, a contextual bandit-based mechanism that dynamically adjusts the relative importance of these signals based on training feedback. Furthermore, a bounded staleness compensation mechanism accounts for historical selection patterns by increasing the selection priority of samples that have not been selected for extended periods. Extensive experiments across diverse vision and language tasks demonstrate the effectiveness and generality of LeDAS. Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, LeDAS consistently achieves superior performance, matching or surpassing full-dataset training at a 50\% selection ratio on ImageNet-1K and in LLM supervised fine-tuning. Moreover, its modular and task-agnostic design enables the integration of complementary selection signals, demonstrating strong robustness to noisy and corrupted datasets.

title: PanoUAV-Track: Full-Spherical UAV Visual Tracking in the Wild
summary: Existing UAV tracking benchmarks predominantly rely on perspective cameras with limited fields of view. Omnidirectional cameras enable full-spherical observation, yet tracking from moving UAV platforms remains largely unexplored. Unlike ground-level panoramic tracking, UAV-mounted omnidirectional cameras observe targets across both azimuth and elevation, introducing geometric challenges under equirectangular projection (ERP). To investigate this setting, we capture approximately \textbf{40 hours of real-world 8K panoramic UAV video} and construct \textbf{PanoUAV-Track} through temporal clip extraction, target annotation, and the integration of simulated sequences. The resulting benchmark comprises 1,895 sequences, 507,961 frames, and 2,872 annotated objects, covering real-world daytime and nighttime scenes alongside simulation, and supporting both visual and language-based target specification. Through extensive evaluations, we reveal a clear \textbf{perspective-to-spherical} generalization gap and identify tracking degradation associated with latitude-dependent distortion and ERP seam discontinuity. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{PanoUAV-Tracker (PUTrack)}, a geometry-aware tracking framework combining latitude-adaptive search and seam-aware periodic sampling. PUTrack improves zero-shot and in-domain tracking, particularly for seam-crossing targets. Code and benchmark resources will be available\footnote{\textcolor{tabpink}{https://libingyu01.github.io/PanoUAV-Track/}}.

title: Embodied-Harness: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Vision-language model (VLM)-based agents offer a promising approach to robotic manipulation, yet remain limited by inadequate memory organization, uncertain failure attribution, and limited reuse of execution experience. We propose Embodied-Harness, a dual-agent framework that improves manipulation by refining the execution harness without updating model parameters. The Actor interacts with the environment through a robot-control interface, while the Reflector converts execution evidence into reusable operational guidance. Hierarchical Memory Architecture maintains short-term execution context and long-term experiential knowledge to support execution and reflection. Evidence-based Experience Reflection grounds failure diagnosis in observed interactions, while Recursive Harness Self-Improvement refines operational guidance across successive attempts. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboSPA, and RMBench demonstrate the effectiveness of Embodied-Harness in generalization under environmental variations, spatial reasoning, long-horizon planning, and memory-dependent manipulation. Our method achieves success rates of 82.4%, 76.7%, and 94.4% on the three benchmarks, respectively. Real-world evaluation further yields an average success rate of 96.7% across three manipulation tasks. These results highlight the potential of Embodied-Harness to improve robotic manipulation through experience-driven harness self-improvement.

title: Taking Apart and Putting Together: Tracking Objects Through Physical Transformations
summary: We introduce Transformation Tracking and Understanding (TTU), extending video object tracking to environments where objects undergo physical assemblies and disassemblies. TTU requires continuously tracking objects through transformations, identifying new entities, maintaining a state graph of their relationships, and assigning semantic labels to transformations. While foundation models (e.g., SAM 2/3) maintain tracklets through appearance changes, they cannot update semantic identities as objects physically evolve. Prior work addresses only disassemblies, relying on expensive searches triggered only when tracking fails. We propose Tracking Instances via Proposals and Overlaps (TIPO), a training-free framework that continuously infers transformations via a generate-evaluate-judge pipeline. TIPO generates split and merge proposals from disjoint mask components, scores them against mask-decoder priors using inner and external overlap, and queries an MLLM on the top proposal for visual verification and semantic labeling. To benchmark TTU, we curate Video Instances, States, and Transformation Annotations (VISTA), a dataset including state graphs with 124 assembly and 132 disassembly events across 50 sequences and over 26,000 frames. TIPO achieves state-of-the-art tracking and state-graph accuracy on VISTA, while operating $6\times$ to $15\times$ faster than prior methods. Project page: https://davidegardenal.github.io/tipo-tracking

title: When Are Images Needed in Multimodal Machine Translation? Text-Only Routing for On-Demand Visual Context
summary: Image-guided multimodal machine translation (MMT) leverages visual context to resolve translation-relevant uncertainty. However, prevailing systems either process images unconditionally or apply gating only after visual encoding, leaving redundant visual computation unavoidable. To mitigate this computational overhead, routing decisions must rely on a pre-visual source signal. Crucially, surface-level ambiguity does not equate to visual dependence, as intra-sentence textual context often suffices for disambiguation. We therefore formulate visual invocation as source-text sufficiency prediction: determining exclusively from the source text whether translation-relevant uncertainty remains unresolved. To support this formulation, we construct a visual-dependency dataset with three fine-grained labels (no_ambiguity, text_resolved, and vision_needed) and verify discriminative visual evidence for vision_needed instances. We further propose PreVIR, a lightweight, backend-agnostic text-only router that selects between text-only and multimodal branches before computing visual features. Experiments on English-to-Chinese MMT demonstrate that PreVIR achieves a favorable COMET-budget trade-off relative to strong routing baselines. At its default operating point, it substantially reduces visual calls while maintaining translation quality comparable to always-on multimodal inference. Label-wise and case analyses show that this trade-off stems from distinguishing genuine visual dependency from contextually resolved ambiguity.

title: Detecting Word-Substitution Poisoning of a RAG Knowledge Base with Relative Entropy and Runtime Verification
summary: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system answers questions using passages it retrieves from a knowledge base, so users must trust that knowledge base. We study an attacker who quietly edits existing passages by swapping words for synonyms (PWWS, TextFooler) in a cybersecurity RAG system built from MITRE ATT&CK and CAPEC. Using a reviewed 44-question benchmark, repeated paired runs and a control corpus in which only the layout changes, we find that poisoning lowers judged answer correctness from 0.714 to 0.555. The damage comes mostly from lost evidence and refusals, not from false statements. To find the edited passages, we use relative entropy. Comparing a whole passage with normal text is a weak signal. Still, one term of the relative entropy, the log-ratio between a word and its most probable synonym, works well: with a small language model as the reference, it reaches an AUROC of 0.95 and stays near chance on the control. Used as a retrieval filter, it halves how often edited text reaches the generator, and an attacker who must keep each passage as probable under the language model fails on all 57 sections it tries. Filtering does not restore correctness, because the edited passage is usually the one that held the answer. We therefore add a runtime monitor that checks each answer against trusted MITRE STIX data and remembers the passages it rejects. On its own, it reduces exposure to edited text from 0.41 to 0.26; when it may add the trusted MITRE entry as a source, correctness rises to 0.786. We report the costs and failure cases of every defence alongside its gains.

title: RoSci: Exploring Robustness in Science VLMs
summary: Recent advancements in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable significant progress in scientific tasks. However, these models are generally assumed to be presented with complete and accurate information, overlooking the challenges of erroneous/missing information in wild scenarios. To address this gap, we introduce the concept of Scientific Model Robustness, which defines a model's ability to detect anomalies, assess solvability, and perform self-calibration when faced with Information Error (inconsistencies) or Information Loss (insufficiency). Specifically, we present RoSci-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,220 samples using a seed-variant strategy across six degradation types. To address VLM fragility, we further propose RoSci-Agent, a framework that employs a Parse-Verify-Decide pipeline to vet premises before reasoning. The evaluated VLMs sometimes answer questions whose premises are invalid or incomplete. RoSci-Agent achieves a higher Overall Robustness Score than the evaluated standalone VLMs. RoSci-Bench gives the multimodal reasoning community a common test of when models answer, request clarification, or reject a scientific question.

title: ADEPT: Adaptive Monocular Depth Estimation via Model-In-The-Loop Photometric Tuning with Capture Risk Prediction
summary: Exposure and gain determine the visual evidence available to monocular depth estimation (MDE), particularly when robot motion creates a tradeoff between light collection and motion blur. We present ADEPT, a framework that adapts these settings using learned feedback from a frozen depth model. During training, ground-truth depth identifies the lowest-error reference within a group of physically evaluated camera settings. A compact predictor learns reference-relative disagreement (RRD) between each candidate's depth prediction and the reference prediction using regression and ranking losses. At deployment, it scores observed captures using frozen-model features and camera, motion, and illumination context, without ground truth or reference images. A contextual Gaussian-process controller uses recent scores to select subsequent exposure and gain settings under motion and photometric constraints. We evaluate offline camera selection with relative and metric Depth Anything v2 and demonstrate online control with the affine-invariant variant on a mobile robot. Across nine equally weighted scene-illumination conditions, ADEPT reduces mean scale-and-shift-aligned $\mathrm{Abs}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ by 14.6% relative to built-in auto-exposure and by 10.0% relative to the best-performing evaluated prior controller.

title: Feasibility of Multifrequency Neural Network-Based Wave Inversion in Ultrasound Time-Harmonic Elastography
summary:
Ultrasound time-harmonic elastography (THE) is a non-invasive imaging technique that measures soft-tissue stiffness. Relying on the same principle of time-harmonic shear wave excitation as established magnetic resonance elastography (MRE), THE offers full field-of-view stiffness mapping at short acquisition times and sub-second temporal resolution across organs. However, reconstruction of shear wave speed maps from acquired tissue wavefields remains challenging due to speckle noise and sparse spatial coverage of the lateral component.
  Deep learning methods have shown promising results for image reconstruction in transient-based ultrasound elastography modalities but remain unexplored in THE. In MRE, MF-ElastoNet, a 2D multifrequency neural network-based wave reconstruction method trained on synthetic physics-based wave data, has shown high generalizability across dynamic ranges and resolutions.
  We investigated the potential of a multifrequency neural network-based wave inversion for THE, by performing a first feasibility analysis. To this end, we adapted the processing pipeline of MF-ElastoNet from MRE to THE. We tested our approach on THE acquired phantom data from the algorithms for mapping elastic modulus Challenge, as well as on in vivo liver THE in 4 healthy volunteers and 14 patients with focal liver lesions, including benign focal nodular hyperplasia, and malignant hepatocellular carcinoma and adenocarcinoma. MF-ElastoNet was successfully adapted to THE with in vivo liver testing. Compared with k-MDEV, the state-of-the-art wave inversion method for THE, Bland-Altman analysis showed a mean bias of -0.02 m/s (95% limits of agreement: -0.36 to 0.33 m/s).

title: TrojanMaxxing: One-shotting VLM Backdoors with Weight-Space Programming
summary: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can reason directly about the weights of other neural networks. Given only a natural-language objective, an LLM can inspect a model's weights, understand what they compute, and edit them directly without gradient-based optimization. This capability, termed weight-space programming (WSP), has been used to improve model performance on math reasoning, medical QA and other benchmarks. We propose TrojanMaxxing, a novel strategy to backdoor vision-language models (VLMs), by reframing it as a WSP task. We use Claude Opus 5.5 and Mythos 5.2 agents to backdoor VLMs without any optimization or training methods. The agents inspect the model weights, apply targeted edits, and co-design an imperceptible visual trigger that activates the backdoor. We then study the agents' strategies and present a thorough evaluation of the trojaned models on various benchmark datasets. TrojanMaxxing achieves attack success rates of 93%-100% on content moderation and 78%-100% on OCR while maintaining clean accuracy. Perhaps most consequentially, we show that injecting backdoors in a training-free manner is possible by simply, "asking an agent to do it".

title: Underwater Spectral Recovery via Multi-View Hyperspectral Imaging
comment: Preprint. Code and data can be shared upon publication. 27 pages (15 main, 12 appendix), 12 figures
summary: Underwater imaging suffers from wavelength-dependent absorption and scattering that distort scenes and obscure spectral signatures. While RGB restoration improves visual clarity, the outputs remain broadband and tied to the sensor's color space. We introduce a physically grounded framework that lifts underwater restoration to continuous spectral radiance using multi-view hyperspectral imaging. By representing continuous spectra via low-rank basis functions and leveraging multi-distance observations, our framework jointly constrains scene radiance and water parameters. We employ a robust sparse-to-dense pipeline: water parameters are estimated from consistent multi-view matches and then applied globally to invert the light transport model across the full images. Validated on physics-based synthetic data rendered via the Mitsuba 3 spectral path tracer, our method recovers physically meaningful radiance spectra and, as a downstream application, outperforms standard image restoration baselines.

title: Cleave: Severing Guardrails and Auditing Spectral Coupling in Open-Weight LLMs
summary: Open-weight Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely downloaded for their strong coding and reasoning capabilities and deployed locally beyond the provider's control. To prevent misuse, developers embed safety guardrails into these models before release. However, we find that these guardrails rely on the residual writing weights to trigger refusals. Based on this insight, we propose Cleave, a training-free attack that directly edits these weights to remove safety restrictions while preserving general capabilities. With Cleave, malicious users can either remove all guardrails or selectively lift only cybersecurity restrictions. Because this selective removal retains up to a 99% refusal rate on other harmful requests and avoids weight rank collapse, it evades both behavioral spot-checks and static weight audits. Across five open-weight LLMs from 7B to 320B parameters, Cleave achieves up to a 67.97% attack success rate on seven safety benchmarks, substantially outperforming existing white-box baselines. On 356 cybersecurity tasks and 15 live vulnerable services, it further boosts executable exploit generation by up to 24.0 times and compromises up to 66.7% of the targets. To counter this threat, we propose a dual-stage defense that combines pre-release subspace diagnostics with post-release weight-coupling audits, achieving 100% detection recall at a 1% false-positive rate.

title: Augmentation of cardiovascular flow measurements with generative diffusion models
summary: Cardiovascular imaging offers several ways to measure blood flow, but each provides an incomplete, resolution-limited, or noisy view of the underlying dynamics. Reconstructing the missing information is inherently ambiguous because several flow fields may be compatible with the same observation. Here, we investigate generative diffusion models as tools for cardiovascular-flow generation and reconstruction using a fully controlled state-of-the-art dataset from a digital twin of a healthy human left heart. First, we show how unconditional samples reproduce the changing anatomy and the highly fluctuating statistical properties of the flow throughout the cardiac cycle. Second, we test the conditional inference of our generative model by reconstructing an entire 2D planar section of geometry and flow configurations from a limited portion. Repeated reconstructions allow us to represent a range of plausible completions, going beyond a single deterministic estimate, while their mean retains the principal features of the reference flow. Comparison with a Gaussian process regression baseline on the same reduced domain highlights the main advantage of diffusion models: their reconstructed ensembles capture a broader range of velocity and gradient fluctuations, better encompassing ground-truth features that the baseline distributions can miss. Our results provide a quantitative proof of concept for probabilistic reconstruction of incomplete cardiovascular-flow measurements and demonstrate the potential for groundbreaking applications to the augmentation of in-vivo cardiovascular imaging data.

title: Neurodegenerative Differential Diagnosis with Knowledge-enhanced Structural Reasoning
summary: Accurate differential diagnosis of neurodegenerative disorders remains challenging due to overlapping clinical manifestations and heterogeneous, often incomplete multimodal observations. Existing multimodal models can integrate imaging and clinical measurements but often overlook disease-specific evidence patterns and pairwise relations among competing diagnoses. We therefore propose Knowledge-enhanced Structural Reasoning (KnowSR), which aligns multimodal patient representations with a literature-grounded knowledge bank of disease prototypes, signed evidence directions, and pairwise diagnostic relations. Specifically, in KnowSR, patient-specific knowledge alignment and target-aware pooling inject structured disease evidence, while anchored relational reasoning reconciles pairwise diagnostic margins over a sparse differential graph, thereby collectively enhancing differential diagnostic capability. Across extensive experiments, KnowSR consistently outperforms 19 baselines on patient-level six-class diagnosis under patient-disjoint five-fold evaluation. This shows that grounding patient evidence in structured medical knowledge enables more effective differential diagnosis than naive multimodal fusion alone.

title: No Audio, No Transcripts, No Problem: LLM-based ASR Adaptation Using Only Domain Documents
summary: Can a speech recognizer be adapted to a new domain with no target audio and no transcripts, using only written documentation? This is the realistic onboarding setting: a new customer hands over raw documentation, not the transcripts that text-only adaptation normally assumes. We turn a domain's documents into adaptation text in two ways, directly as written sentences or rendered by a large language model (LLM) into synthetic spoken dialogs, and feed them to a recently proposed denoising-based text-only adaptation method. We show that, across in-domain, out-of-domain, and cross-domain settings on two corpora, document-only adaptation can match or closely approach real transcriptions; whether written or conversational rendering is best depends on speaking style and the amount of text generated. To our knowledge, this is the first study of document-only adaptation of LLM-based ASR. As no existing corpus pairs audio, transcripts, and documents, we also built and released a document-grounded benchmark.

title: THRIFTY: Cost-Constrained Reasoning-Data Synthesis for Small Language Models
comment: Published at the Efficient Reasoning Workshop, COLM 2026
summary: Small language models (SLMs) are increasingly attractive for efficient, specialized deployment, and are typically trained on reasoning trajectories distilled from a larger teacher LLM. Generating this synthetic data is a major cost of the pipeline, especially when the teacher is a frontier model. Existing collection methods, however, are largely cost-unaware, or at best spread a fixed sampling budget uniformly across queries. Such allocation ignores the wide variation in problem difficulty and the strategic over- or under-sampling it invites. Thus, we propose THRIFTY, a Thompson-sampling bandit controller that spends a fixed generation-token budget to collect diverse correct reasoning trajectories, casting the task as a bandits-with-knapsacks problem with a novel diversity-aware objective. It tracks each problem's success probability with an online Beta posterior and spends each token where it expects the most new distinct correct solutions. Because repeated solutions add progressively less value, THRIFTY adaptively stops resampling saturated problems, concentrates budget on under-covered ones, and retires the unsolvable at the budget's opportunity cost. On math (AIME, MATH-500) and code (LiveCodeBench) benchmarks, THRIFTY gathers up to 22% more diverse correct trajectories per generation token than both the standard uniform-sampling recipe and the strongest adaptive baseline, with the largest gains in the scarce-budget and hard-problem regimes.

title: Learning When to Ask: Advisor-Aware Post-Training for SLM Agents
comment: Published at the OE-Agent Workshop (Open and Efficient Agentic AI for Resource-Constrained Environments) at ACML 2026 14 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables
summary: Small language models (SLMs) are increasingly attractive for cheap, high-throughput agentic deployment, but they remain weak at multi-step reasoning and tool use that long-horizon tasks demand. We study how to post-train an SLM to seek advice from a stronger model and act on that advice itself, following an advisor-executor pattern. Out of the box, this pattern fails across open- and closed-source small-model families: wiring an SLM to an advisor is a harness-design matter that is not enough on its own. A post-training recipe is needed to teach the model when to ask, in a cost-aware fashion, and how to follow advice across steps. Our method, ADAPT (ADvisor-Aware Post-Training), is a multi-stage recipe that instills this behavior, learning entirely from the policy's own rollouts supervised by the environment's outcome, with no learned reward model or human annotation. Across three domains, compared to an untrained harness baseline, ADAPT improves success rate in embodied text reasoning (TextWorld) from 24.5% to 77.3%, code generation (LiveCodeBench) from 21.8% to 56.0%, and deep web search (GAIA) from 17.5% to 49.3%, while querying the advisor sparingly (~1.0-2.1 calls per task). On the two long-horizon domains it closes 70-85% of the gap to an oracle that perfectly times when to ask for advice, and on code generation it exceeds that oracle. The gains persist when the advisor is replaced by one unseen in training, showing that the learned help-seeking policy is robust to a changing advisor rather than tied to the one it was trained with.

title: Mechanism Parity for Simulation-Based Validation of Autonomous-Driving Perception
comment: 15 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Extended version of the authors' papers at IEEE IV 2026 and IEEE ITSC 2026. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Simulation is central to intelligent-vehicle validation, but visual realism or output agreement between a real scene and its synthetic counterpart does not prove that a perception system used the same evidence in both domains. This paper addresses that mechanism-parity gap for paired real-synthetic autonomous-driving perception. It unifies Decisive-Feature Fidelity, which compares decisive evidence maps in a frozen system under test (SUT), with Concept-Decisive Feature Fidelity, which projects decisive evidence into semantic scene concepts for diagnosis. The framework is a validation diagnostic rather than a standalone safety certificate: it asks whether output-consistent simulation also preserves the mechanism by which the perception model reaches that output. The empirical evidence comprises ten retrained diffusion ControlNet generators evaluated on a deterministic exact-geometry KITTI-Virtual KITTI 2 subset. Generated counterparts use a 1248-by-376-pixel padded inference canvas and are cropped back to the exact KITTI dimensions before evaluation. The final benchmark reports target-image, output-consistency, and mechanism metrics recomputed from a single audited output set, then adds metric-disagreement cases, bootstrap uncertainty, threshold sensitivity, and concept/cache integrity audits. Across the benchmark, output and appearance fidelity are at most weakly and inconsistently rank-correlated with decisive-mechanism distance for all three frozen SUTs, and a constructed positive control shows the estimator detects a known planted mechanism that output agreement misses, supporting decisive-evidence diagnostics for intelligent-vehicle simulation validation. All numerical claims are restricted to the declared exact-geometry benchmark, ten generators, and three frozen SUTs.

title: On the Challenges of Using LLMs in High-Risk AI Recruitment: Guiding Questions for Legal Conformity with the AI Act
comment: 54 pages, 3 figures, 9 tables. Submitted to Ethics and Information Technology (Springer) for review
summary: The EU Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) imposes detailed obligations on providers of high-risk AI systems but offers limited operational guidance, particularly when these systems integrate third-party General-Purpose AI (GPAI) models. This paper introduces a toolkit that fosters the development of legal-by-design AI-assisted recruitment systems by translating the core legal obligations of the AI Act's conformity assessment---specifically Articles 9--15 and Annex IV---into techno-normative requirements and corresponding guiding questions. While recruitment pipelines may involve components with varying technical complexity and differing levels of algorithmic transparency, this paper focuses on the most challenging case: the integration of third-party GPAI models into critical stages of the selection process, including resume and job description parsing, applicant scoring, and shortlist generation. This scenario presents significant challenges for downstream providers of high-risk AI systems, as it underscores the difficulties in obtaining the technical information needed to demonstrate compliance with the AI Act's techno-normative requirements, both prior to and during market deployment. After introducing the toolkit and illustrating its application through a simplified example, the paper explores informational dependencies between upstream and downstream GPAI model providers. These dependencies may produce informational gaps across the AI supply chain, potentially hindering the collection of evidence necessary for the AI system provider to ensure legal compliance. The resulting lack of technical transparency negatively affects the deployer, who may struggle to maintain meaningful oversight of the system, and ultimately impacts the persons subject to the AI output.

title: Cecilia: Towards Layout-Inclusive Optical Music Recognition
summary: Reconstructing an editable music score requires musical events, sung text and the instructions that organise them on the page. Existing recognition targets often omit part of this information, while direct MusicXML prediction repeats substantial structural markup. We introduce Cecilia, a compact representation of canonicalised MusicXML that retains musical content, lyric attachments and layout instructions. Cecilia-OMR predicts this representation through metadata and measure-bounded music segments from shared visual memory. A learned count head determines the number of output segments. Across paired complete scores under a common tokeniser, the ratio of mean MusicXML to Cecilia sequence lengths is 27.73. Cecilia-OMR outperforms Legato 2 on Camera String Quartets and both Lieder conditions, with a four-condition OpenScore macro normalised edit distance of 0.2232 against 0.2998. Separate evaluations of lyrics, notation trees and rendered layout reveal complementary aspects of reconstruction and quantify the contribution of layout instructions. Training-stage, reward and candidate-selection studies further examine how recognition changes across model adaptation and decoding.

title: ROSWORLD: When Digital Task Competence Meets Physical Execution
summary: Computer-use agents now solve most desktop tasks through direct software input, but a robot using the same computer must turn GUI knowledge into physical contact with a keyboard and mouse. We introduce ROSWorld, a benchmark that couples a physically simulated robot workstation to a live OSWorld desktop, so that a robot and a desktop agent pursue the same goals under the same official evaluators. The evaluated model receives observations only from the workstation camera views and operates the peripherals through either a single-arm rigid probe or dual-arm dexterous hands. Across five frontier models and 40 tasks in ten applications, models that complete 31-39 tasks on the desktop complete at most 23 with the probe and 28 with the hands. Paired trajectory analysis shows that models adapt their interaction strategies toward keyboard input, yet physical execution frequently fails through missed presses, incorrect targets, and unintended contacts. ROSWorld makes the gap between knowing what to do on a computer and physically doing it measurable.

title: Alignment without Transfer: Tokenization Impacts Cross-lingual Representations during Multilingual Language Model Pretraining
summary: Tokenization represents one of the most crucial steps in mulilingual NLP pipelines. Yet, tokenizers routinely under-allocate vocabulary to low-resource languages. While improved allocation leads to better performance, it remains poorly understood how tokenization shapes cross-lingual representations and transfer during pretraining. To address this, we pretrain 39 mono- and bilingual 1B decoder-only models on FineWeb2-HQ across English, German, French, Arabic and Chinese, varying only the tokenizer. Our results demonstrate that improved vocabulary allocation (i) substantially raises cross-lingual representation alignment in early-to-mid layers, an effect that prior work measuring only the output layer could not observe, (ii) increases cross-lingual parametric knowledge sharing in feed-forward neurons, supported by correlational and causal evidence, and (iii) an alignment-transfer dissociation, where cross-lingual transfer remains essentially unchanged despite higher alignment. Moreover, transfer is significantly lower for cross-script bilinguals even under fair vocabulary allocation, indicating that the script barrier is not merely a tokenizer artifact. All of our checkpoints and code are publicly available.

title: Learning Unknown Oscillators From Bandit Feedback
summary: We study semi-bandits driven by unknown oscillators. Each round, a learner selects two of four reward channels and observes their individual rewards. Frequency errors change future reward rankings and the resulting measurements. We show when committing to one fitted oscillator lets its greedy choices expose prediction errors. Our controller bounds reward loss (regret) over a continuous confidence set and holds the longest block within budget. An online regression policy gathers observations when the check fails. Regret grows at a square-root rate, up to logarithmic factors, across all frequencies and extends to two competing oscillators. On 96 fresh synthetic instances, checked commitment uses 49 fits instead of 1,023, with 1.5% higher mean regret than fitting every round. Matched isolated timings give a 4.69-fold speedup. The confidence sets also certify trajectory regret.

title: Turnout: Adaptive Attention Switching for Efficient Reasoning
summary: Post-hoc transformer linearization replaces the key-value cache of full attention, which grows linearly with generation length, with a fixed size state. This change reduces memory consumption but often hurts accuracy. In reasoning tasks, which require long generations, this effect is especially pronounced. In this work we introduce Turnout, a method that mitigates accuracy loss as a result of linearization, while maintaining its memory-reduction benefits. We apply post-hoc linearization to a pretrained full-attention model, training a linear path through distillation while leaving the original full-attention path unchanged. During response generation, the resulting hybrid model retains both paths and uses a learned policy to control when each layer switches from full to linear attention. We train the policy with reinforcement learning using a reward that balances answer correctness and memory use. Empirical evaluation of our method shows that the learned adaptive policy achieves a better accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier on reasoning tasks compared to fixed switching and static hybrid baselines.

title: The Assistant Persona Differs Across Languages in Activation Space
summary: Large language models behave differently across languages, and are noticeably less safe in lower-resource languages. This gap is well established behaviorally, but not mechanistically. Directions in activation space, including the assistant persona direction, are almost always extracted from English and assumed to generalize across languages. We extract the assistant persona direction in 31 languages in Qwen3-32B, and find that the resulting axes differ substantially: their cosine similarity to the English axis ranges from 0.378 to 0.911. Moreover, each language's assistant persona direction and its magnitude are correlated with the language's resource level. We also find that the model's default assistant state is farther from the helpful assistant pole in lower-resource languages. Finally, steering against a language's own axis amplifies persona-based jailbreak more than steering against the English axis. These results indicate that the model does not carry a single assistant representation across languages. More broadly, the assistant persona may need to be an explicit target of multilingual alignment.

title: Self-Supervised Continuous-Time Depth Learning and Ego-Motion Estimation from Asynchronous Events
summary: Event cameras register brightness changes pixel by pixel with microsecond precision, whereas the dense depth that could supervise them is costly to acquire and exists only at isolated instants. Condensing the stream into frames eases learning, but at the expense of the very timing that sets event sensing apart. We propose a self-supervised approach in which each event is assigned its own depth in continuous time, and the camera motion is recovered from the same observations. Supervision arises from geometry: lifted into 3D by its predicted depth and displaced by the camera motion at the instant it fired, an event should coincide with others produced by the same edge, so any misalignment exposes an error in depth or motion. Differentiable rendering then turns these per-event estimates into dense depth maps at target times within each window, faithful to the events behind them. On MVSEC, the approach outperforms prior event-only self-supervised methods in most sequences and depth ranges, with the widest margins at night, and recovers camera rotation more accurately than an earlier unsupervised event-based method. Ablations isolate the roles of local spatiotemporal context, the temporal backbone, and the alignment objective. These results position motion-compensated event alignment as a principled source of supervision for continuous-time depth and ego-motion estimation.

title: PhiJEPA: Denoising Latent Predictions for Visual Representation Learning
summary: Can a predictor trained to infer hidden image regions still help a world model plan when part of an object disappears from view and the visible context is blurred? We introduce PhiJEPA, a joint-embedding predictive architecture that adapts PhiNet's two-stage prediction to masked Transformers. From sparse, photometrically corrupted context, a Transformer block predicts hidden tokens of an independently corrupted teacher view. A token-wise MLP then maps these predictions to clean teacher tokens. Controlled ablations show that the combined objective improves dense features over the tested one-stage alternatives. Pre-trained on ImageNet-1K with $5.6\times10^{19}$ training FLOPs, PhiJEPA achieves 69.3 mIoU on linear PASCAL VOC segmentation, exceeding the evaluated I-JEPA and DSeq-JEPA checkpoints in segmentation accuracy, with 25\% fewer training FLOPs than I-JEPA. It also improves hidden-region segmentation over Simple I-JEPA (49.1 vs.\ 44.3 mIoU). As an application, we use the frozen encoder in DINO-WM on PushT, and reuse the pre-training predictor, which JEPAs usually discard, to complete occluded tokens without fine-tuning. In open-loop planning with simultaneous object occlusion and Gaussian blur ($σ=2$ pixels), predictor completion raises success from 33\% to 65\%, compared with 25\% for Simple I-JEPA with its predictor and 40\% for iBOT with pixel inpainting. Together, these results support two-stage latent prediction as an efficient approach to learning visual representations that remain useful under photometric degradation and support completion under partial observation.

title: PaMuk-Bench: A Parallel Multilingual Multitask Benchmark for Vision-Language Tasks
summary: While vision-language models (VLMs) currently obtain notable results for highly-studied languages, e.g. English, they exhibit significant performance drops in certain low-resource languages, especially due to the lack of annotated datasets. To this end, we propose PaMuk-Bench, a novel parallel multilingual multitask benchmark for vision-language tasks. Our benchmark includes a set of over 10K curated English prompts that are translated into six languages: Arabic, Danish, French, Hindi, Italian, Romanian. Parallel translations, which are obtained via a semi-automatic process, along with accompanying generated and retrieved images enable the comparative development and evaluation of VLMs across a wide range of tasks: text-to-image generation, image captioning, content-based image retrieval, image generation difficulty estimation, image retrieval difficulty estimation. We empirically show that zero-shot English and multilingual pre-trained VLMs compare consistently worse than their fine-tuned counterparts, confirming that PaMuk-Bench is a valuable resource that can drastically reduce the language gap across a variety of VLM architectures and tasks. PaMuk-Bench is available at https://github.com/ghesil/pamuk_bench.

title: Fix Where It Fails: Root-Cause-Guided Agentic Harness Optimization for Scene Graph Generation
summary: Scene graph generation (SGG) aims to detect objects in an image and predict the relationships between them. The standard PredCls, SGCls, and SGDet settings show how much performance drops without ground-truth boxes and labels, but not where or why a model fails. Knowing this would allow fixing a model where it fails, without retraining. We propose RoHa-SGG (Root-cause-guided Harness optimization for SGG), which extends agentic harness optimization to SGG. It optimizes the harness, the inference code around a frozen SGG model. RoHa-SGG has two main LLM agents. A root-cause analysis (RCA) agent finds the components where the model fails and diagnoses why, and a proposer agent searches for a harness that fixes these causes. We evaluate RoHa-SGG on Visual Genome and PSG with representative two-stage, one-stage, and multimodal-LLM SGG models. The analysis shows that the components where ground-truth triplets are lost differ across models and datasets. RoHa-SGG improves every metric on all five model-dataset combinations. Graph-constrained R@100 and mR@100 rise by up to 15.8 and 26.4 points for the multimodal LLM and by up to 3.6 and 10.1 points for the two-stage and one-stage models. With root-cause guidance, the harness search reaches the final score of an unguided search up to three times faster.

title: On the Limits of Observability for Evaluating Coverage in Machine Unlearning
summary: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of any requested subset of training data while preserving utility on the remaining data. Empirical evaluations measure predictive accuracy and infer training-set membership (MIAs) from model outputs or intermediate activations. However, by focusing on selected forget sets, these evaluations can overlook Coverage, the range of requests a method can fulfill. To assess this coverage, we first conduct a stress test of observability with 502 retrained models, finding that hidden embeddings reveal known deletions missed in predictions. To characterize capacity limits on coverage, we show that distinguishing all $n$ singleton deletions with linear scores can require a shared representation of rank $Ω(\log n)$. We further extend the bound to arbitrary subsets and show when partial deletion can appear complete. Building on this analysis, we propose CEO, a framework for evaluating unlearning coverage under limited observability. Its compositional color-shape benchmark makes forgetting and retained utility measurable from the full output distribution and provides a leave-one-out retraining oracle for each target. From a fixed number of oracle observables, we estimate empirical target coverage, the fraction of targets reliably flagged when deleted and rarely flagged under any other deletions. To recover missed deletions, CEO further expands each observable representation into high-dimensional activation space with the frozen encoder of a SAE trained on the original model. Extensive experiments of 20 baselines shows that even on this simple synthetic task, only retraining from scratch covers all deletion targets.

title: Bringing AI Assistance to the Beznau Nuclear Power Plant: A Hierarchical System of LLM Agents for Reactor Monitoring
summary: Beznau Unit 1 in Switzerland, in operation since 1969, is the most experienced nuclear reactor still running worldwide. Five decades of incremental modernization have left its monitoring systems, alarm logs, variable catalogs, technical specifications and investigation reports in separate silos that were never designed to be queried together. As a result, investigating a core instrumentation anomaly means slow, manual gathering of knowledge scattered across databases, documents, and experienced colleagues. We present a hierarchical multi-agent assistant built on large language models (LLMs) to support these investigations and reduce the need for tedious manual searches in SAP systems. An orchestrating agent breaks down an engineer's question and hands the parts to specialized sub-agents, each with read-only access to one source. Domain expertise is written as natural-language procedures that plant engineers can read, review and revise. The system is strictly advisory, with every answer traced back to its sources. We also report organizational lessons from introducing agentic AI into a culture built on safety, traceability and conservative change. Beyond the technical architecture, the Beznau case study examines how an assistant can be introduced into a setting where evidence must be traceable, changes carefully reviewed, and operational decisions retained by plant personnel, paving the way for the responsible use of agentic AI in industrial plant monitoring.

title: Unlocking Heterogeneous Accelerator Flexibility in AI Data Centers: Sizing and Workload Allocation
summary: AI data centers are an emerging electricity demand, but limited local grid capacity could delay their connection and expansion. While existing operational strategies consider spatio-temporal workload flexibility, few studies address the strategic sizing and allocation of diverse accelerator archetypes with different capital and energy-efficiency trade-offs. This paper unlocks the flexibility potential of heterogeneous accelerators by jointly sizing and allocating different AI workloads (training, delay-tolerant batch work, and online inference requests) across sites and hours to meet the time-varying grid constraint at minimum cost. Workload-specific throughput and energy coefficients link these decisions to facility power.
